lesson_title: Soup Bowl or Fly Cover: Sketching the Parabola
hook_text: Two numbers. One bowl. That's the whole parabola question — and most people only look at one of them.
clip_script: Kick a soccer ball across a field. Up, over the top, down — and the way down mirrors the way up exactly. That shape is a parabola, and in Grade 10 it comes with just two numbers to read. Picture a bowl on your kitchen table. The first number is the one multiplying the squared part, and its SIGN turns the bowl over. Positive, and it stays the right way up, holding soup, with a lowest point. Negative, and the whole thing flips like a dish covering food from the flies — now it has a highest point. Its SIZE decides the shape: bigger than one and the sides climb fast, tall and narrow like a vase; a fraction like a half and it spreads out flat and wide like a serving dish. The second number, sitting on its own at the end, does something completely different — it picks the whole bowl up and moves it straight up or down. Add four and it's on a shelf. Subtract eight and it drops into a hole. And that number is a free gift: it's exactly where the curve crosses the vertical axis, AND the height of the turning point. Now the clever bit. An upright bowl lifted above the line can never touch the line — no crossings at all. Drop the same bowl into a hole and the rim pokes through on both sides — two crossings. Same shape, different height, completely different answer.
visual_style: A kitchen table in warm light: a bowl rotating upright and inverted, stretching tall then flattening wide, then lifting onto a shelf and sinking into a hole while a parabola traces over it on a grid.
pacing: Easy through the ball's arc, crisp beats on each bowl transformation, a pause before the no-crossings reveal.
